rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting the late-elution penalty. Use the observed elution window to focus subsequent gradients.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; shorten the gradient to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed tests slope sensitivity, with the closest pair currently at R = 2.68.
Test the next shorter gradient to locate the speed limit at 40 C. The critical pair is approaching R = 1.5, so this may sacrifice resolution; injection 2 remains a maximum-score fallback.

Test whether higher temperature restores selectivity for the critical pair while further shortening retention. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect; injection 2 remains the faster proven maximum-score method.

Test the opposite temperature direction: cooling may widen the critical middle pair and avoids the early-pair convergence seen at 60 C. The six-minute gradient leaves ample room below the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Use an intermediate temperature to avoid the early-pair coelution at 60 C, and narrow the gradient window to improve middle-pair resolution. Raising the starting organic fraction should also reduce time spent before the first peak.

Make the gradient slightly shallower to lift the critical middle pair above R = 1.5 while retaining the favorable early-pair separation at 50 C. The last peak previously eluted near organic fraction 0.52, so the lower endpoint still leaves ample elution strength.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness to protect the middle pair. Check whether the early pair retains its current resolution margin.

Shift the start upward to shorten retention, while lowering the endpoint one step to improve the marginal middle-pair resolution. Monitor the early pair for compression as the starting solvent becomes stronger.

Lower the endpoint one step to make the gradient shallower and recover the small resolution deficit in the middle pair. Keep the starting fraction and temperature fixed to preserve the early-pair separation.

With maximum-score methods secured, test a much steeper gradient at low temperature for a faster separation after a possible middle-pair order reversal. The broad solvent range should still elute all six compounds promptly.

Explore the fast-gradient regime with a higher starting organic fraction to alter middle-pair selectivity. A moderate temperature increase may improve the late pair that was insufficiently resolved at 25 C.

Return to the fully resolved region with a four-minute gradient whose slope lies between injections 9 and 10, targeting R just above 1.5. The endpoint remains above the observed last-peak elution fraction, so all six peaks should remain within the gradient.

Seek a more robust maximum-score method by slightly flattening injection 8’s gradient, where the middle pair had only R = 1.58. The lower starting fraction than injection 13 also preserves more retention and separation for the early peaks.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to preserve middle-pair resolution. Lowering temperature to 45 C should help retain and separate the early peaks that stronger starting solvent may otherwise compress.

Lower the endpoint from injection 13 by one step to increase the middle-pair resolution margin while keeping the early peaks retained. This tests a compact gradient window expected to preserve the maximum CRF with all peaks eluting well before ten minutes.

Test whether a stronger starting solvent produces a useful middle-pair order reversal in the fast-gradient regime. Low temperature should help retain the early compounds, though early-pair compression remains a risk; maximum-score methods are already secured.

Increase the starting fraction one grid step to test whether the reversed middle pair separates further in the fast-gradient regime. The early pair has some resolution margin, but its compression will determine whether this route remains viable.

Keep the starting fraction fixed and make the fast gradient shallower to test whether the middle pair gains the missing resolution. Avoid raising phi0 further because the first peak is already essentially unretained.

Halve the slope again to seek the remaining middle-pair resolution, keeping temperature and starting fraction fixed. The final hold may delay the last peak, but the previous 2.45-minute elution leaves substantial room below the ten-minute penalty threshold.

Trim injection 14’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting fraction, temperature, and gradient slope. This should retain its maximum CRF and resolution margin with a shorter programmed gradient.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 21 to test a faster separation at the resolution boundary. The middle pair’s R = 1.85 provides some margin, while injection 13 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Lower the starting fraction from injection 22 to improve middle-pair selectivity while keeping the gradient slope unchanged. This should also increase early-pair retention and may provide a fully resolved four-minute gradient with better resolution margins.

Test a cooler, shallower variant of injection 21 to increase early-pair separation while compensating for the middle pair’s temperature sensitivity. This seeks another maximum-score method with useful resolution margins; injection 13 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 24 to shorten elution while using its middle-pair resolution margin of R = 2.19. This final refinement targets maximum CRF at 45 C; injection 13 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.
